transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?

My sleep has been all over the place—some nights I’m up planning and working on music, and other nights I can’t sleep at all or I sleep half the day. It's just gotten really hard to keep any kind of normal routine lately.
During those nights when you are up planning and working on music, do you feel full of energy and find that you need much less sleep than usual to feel rested?

Yeah, exactly. During those bursts I’ll only sleep three or four hours, but I wake up buzzing with ideas and feeling totally fine, like sleep is just an inconvenience getting in the way of my projects.
Have you also experienced periods where you felt the exact opposite—feeling very down, empty, or losing all interest in your music and other activities?

Yes, definitely. I'll wake up with this heavy, sinking feeling in my chest like I've already failed, and I just lie on the couch for days feeling like I'm moving through mud. During those times, I completely lose interest in my coding and music, barely even touching my guitar and just abandoning all my plans.
When you experience these down periods where you feel like you're moving through mud, how long do they typically last?

This current heavy stretch has been hanging over me for about three months now, ever since my long-term contract fell through. Looking back, though, I've been cycling through these shutdown lows and high-energy spurts on and off since my early twenties.
When you have those high-energy bursts where you feel buzzed and need very little sleep, how many days in a row do those periods typically last?
I'm not entirely sure of the exact number of days because I haven't really tracked it closely. Usually, though, those high-energy stretches last for a few days at a time before I start to slow down.
During these down periods, like the current three-month stretch, do you experience severe symptoms such as feelings of worthlessness, excessive guilt, or thoughts of death or suicide?

Yes, I do. I often wake up with this heavy, sinking feeling in my chest, like I’ve already failed before the day even starts. I just lie there staring at the ceiling, thinking my wife would be much better off without me dragging us down like this.
During those high-energy periods, did your behavior ever cause major problems in your relationships or work, or did it ever lead to you being hospitalized?

I’ve never been hospitalized, but those high-energy periods definitely cause a lot of problems for me. I end up straining my marriage because I snap at my wife over the budget and constantly talk over her. On top of that, I jump between unfinished projects, miss deadlines, and lose track of our bills, which has really hurt our finances.
What is the longest one of these high-energy periods has ever lasted for you—has it ever gone on for a full week or more?
I'm not entirely sure if they've ever gone on for a full week, to be honest. I've never really timed those periods, so I don't know exactly how many days they last when I get into that zone.

During those high-energy periods, did your family, friends, or doctors ever become so concerned about your safety or behavior that they felt you needed urgent professional help or evaluation, even if you weren't hospitalized?

No, nobody has ever felt I was in immediate danger or needed urgent psychiatric intervention during those high times. My wife did urge me to get help recently because she's worried about our financial stability and my job search, but it's never been a safety crisis.
During those high-energy periods, did you ever experience things like hearing voices, or have beliefs that others found highly unrealistic, such as having special powers or a unique mission?

No, I've never heard voices or believed I had supernatural powers or some kind of special mission. But I do get highly unrealistic ideas about what I can achieve, like thinking I have this "special grind mode" where I can build an app, launch a YouTube channel, and fix all our money problems overnight.
During those high-energy periods, did the difficulties with your work or finances ever lead to major consequences like losing a job, facing legal issues, or being completely unable to function?

I haven't faced any legal issues, but these ups and downs have caused some really serious problems. I've blown past job application deadlines, missed a deadline for a promising internship, and we've fallen behind on rent because I lost track of bills. It's made our financial situation much worse and left me feeling completely stuck.
Can you recall any specific time in your life when one of these high-energy periods lasted for a full week (7 days) or longer?

I'm not entirely sure because I've never tracked the exact number of days. They definitely feel like they go on for several days at a time, but I can't say for certain if they've ever lasted a full week.
Have you ever had a high-energy period where your behavior was so extreme or chaotic that you were completely unable to carry out any daily activities or work at all for several days in a row?

No, during those high-energy times I’m actually extremely active and constantly working on projects, even if I'm jumping from task to task without finishing them. It's only when I crash into my low, depressed periods that I completely shut down and can't do basic daily activities or work.

During those high-energy periods, did your disorganization or impulsive decisions ever lead to major consequences like getting fired from a job, or did you always manage to keep things from completely falling apart?

I haven't been fired from a traditional job since I mostly do freelance work, but things definitely fall apart because I start a ton of projects and business plans at once and never actually finish them. That disorganization, combined with the crash that follows, has made me blow past application deadlines and lose track of bills, which is why we've fallen behind on rent.

During those high-energy periods, did you ever engage in risky or impulsive behaviors, such as reckless driving, unusual spending sprees, or making major financial commitments that you couldn't afford?

I don't recall doing anything really reckless like speeding or going on big spending sprees during those high times. I do tend to get overly ambitious, though, and end up taking on way too many projects at once thinking I can fix our money problems overnight.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a history of recurrent mood disturbances characterized by both major depressive episodes and hypomanic episodes, which is diagnostic of Bipolar II disorder (classified under F31.8, Other bipolar affective disorders, in ICD-10). He is currently experiencing a severe depressive episode of three months' duration, marked by depressed mood, anhedonia, psychomotor retardation, and thoughts of being a burden to his wife. He also describes clear, distinct periods of hypomania characterized by a decreased need for sleep, increased goal-directed activity, grandiosity ('special grind mode'), distractibility, and irritability. These high periods last for several days but do not meet the 7-day duration or severity criteria (no hospitalization, no psychosis, no complete loss of functioning) required for a manic episode (ruling out Bipolar I). The severity of the depressive symptoms rules out Cyclothymia (F34.0).
